sources.title: OpenStax: Moment of inertia and rotational kinetic energy
OpenStax: Newton's second law for rotation

chapters.title: Same angle, different distances
chapters.formula: s = r theta; v = r omega
points: Angles must be in radians in these equations.
All points on a rigid wheel share its angular velocity.
At r = 0.5 m and omega = 4 rad/s, tangential speed is 2 m/s.
chapters.script: Welcome back. Imagine a wheel turning about a fixed axle. A dot near the rim travels farther than a dot near the centre during the same turn. Yet both dots turn through the same angle. That distinction is the starting point of rotation. We measure angular displacement in radians. One radian means the arc length equals the radius. So arc length equals radius times angular displacement, provided the angle is in radians. A point half a metre from the axle turns through two radians. Its arc length is one metre. Notice that this is distance along a circular arc, not the straight line displacement between its endpoints. Angular velocity tells us how quickly the angle changes. We call it omega. Tangential speed equals radius times omega. If our wheel turns at four radians per second, the dot half a metre from the axle moves at two metres per second. What about a dot halfway to that rim? Take a moment. It has the same angular velocity, but half the tangential speed. In JEE questions, always distinguish angular quantities from linear quantities, and check which radius belongs to the point being discussed.

chapters.title: Torque is the turning effect of a force
chapters.formula: tau = r F sin(theta) = F d(perpendicular)
points: Measure the position vector from the chosen axis.
The lever arm is the perpendicular distance to the force's line of action.
20 N perpendicular to a 0.25 m wrench gives 5 N m.
chapters.script: Why is a long wrench easier to turn than a short one? The turning effect of a force depends not only on the force, but also on where and how it acts. That turning effect is torque. For motion in a plane, the torque magnitude about a chosen axis is radius times force times sine of the angle between them. Here radius means the position vector from the axis to the point where the force acts. An equivalent method is force times the perpendicular distance from the axis to the force's line of action. That distance is the lever arm. Push perpendicular to a wrench, twenty five centimetres from the bolt, with twenty newtons. Convert the length to zero point two five metres. The torque is five newton metres. Now push directly along the wrench toward the bolt. Predict the torque before calculating. It is zero, because the force's line of action passes through the axis. Choose an anticlockwise positive sign, then add clockwise torques with a negative sign. Torque uses newton metres, but we do not call it energy in joules: torque describes turning tendency, while work describes energy transfer.

chapters.title: Mass distribution controls rotational inertia
chapters.formula: I = sum(m r squared); ring: MR squared; disk: (1/2)MR squared
points: Moment of inertia depends on the chosen axis.
A 1 kg point mass at 0.5 m has I = 0.25 kg m squared.
Ring and uniform disk formulas here use the central perpendicular axis.
chapters.script: Mass tells us how strongly an object resists a change in linear motion. For rotation, we also need to know where that mass sits relative to the axis. This is moment of inertia, represented by capital I. For point particles, add each mass multiplied by the square of its perpendicular distance from the axis. A one kilogram point mass half a metre from the axis contributes zero point two five kilogram metres squared. Move it to one metre, and the contribution becomes one kilogram metre squared. Doubling the distance has quadrupled the moment of inertia. That squared distance is the reason mass near the rim matters so much. For a thin ring about its central perpendicular axis, the moment of inertia is mass times radius squared. For a uniform solid disk about the equivalent axis, it is one half mass times radius squared. The disk has some mass closer to the centre, so its moment of inertia is smaller for the same mass and radius. These formulas are not interchangeable, and changing the axis changes the answer. Before using a formula in an exam, identify the shape, the mass distribution, and the axis explicitly.

chapters.title: From net torque to angular acceleration
chapters.formula: tau(net) = I alpha; omega = omega(0) + alpha t
points: Fixed-axis rigid disk: M = 2 kg, R = 0.5 m, I = 0.25 kg m squared.
Constant net torque 1 N m gives alpha = 4 rad/s squared.
From rest after 3 s: omega = 12 rad/s; angle = 18 rad; K = 18 J.
chapters.script: Now combine the ideas in a worked problem. A uniform solid disk rotates about a fixed axle through its centre, perpendicular to its face. Its mass is two kilograms and its radius is half a metre. A constant net torque of one newton metre acts on it. It starts from rest. Find its angular speed after three seconds. First calculate the moment of inertia: one half times two times half squared gives zero point two five kilogram metres squared. For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, net torque about that axis equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration. Divide one by zero point two five. The angular acceleration is four radians per second squared. Constant angular acceleration means we can use the rotational version of our straight line equations. Final angular velocity equals initial angular velocity plus angular acceleration times time. Starting from rest gives twelve radians per second after three seconds. The angle turned is one half alpha t squared, or eighteen radians. Here is an energy check. Rotational kinetic energy is one half I omega squared, giving eighteen joules. Constant torque times angular displacement also gives eighteen joules of work. Two approaches agree. Remember: the torque supplied in this question is the net torque, after including any opposing torques.

chapters.title: Rolling combines translation and rotation
chapters.formula: v(cm) = R omega; K = (1/2)M v(cm) squared + (1/2)I(cm) omega squared
points: The no-slip relation assumes rolling on a stationary surface.
A 2 kg uniform disk rolling at 2 m/s has total K = 6 J.
An equal-mass thin ring at the same centre speed has total K = 8 J.
chapters.script: A wheel rolling along the ground does two things: its centre moves forward, and the wheel rotates about its centre. We must include both parts of the kinetic energy. Translational energy is one half mass times centre speed squared. Rotational energy is one half moment of inertia about the centre times angular speed squared. For rolling without slipping on a stationary surface, centre speed equals radius times angular speed. Do not apply that constraint to a wheel that is skidding. Try a uniform solid disk of mass two kilograms and radius half a metre, rolling without slipping at a centre speed of two metres per second. Its angular speed is four radians per second. Translational energy is four joules. Its moment of inertia is zero point two five kilogram metres squared, so rotational energy is two joules. Total kinetic energy is six joules. What changes for a thin ring with the same mass, radius, and centre speed? Pause and compare the moments of inertia. The ring has twice the rotational inertia, so its rotational energy is four joules and its total is eight joules. That does not mean it has a greater centre speed; the speeds were specified equal. Your final checklist is axis, torque, moment of inertia, and any rolling constraint. These are foundations; angular momentum, axis theorems, and more advanced rolling problems need further study.

quiz.question: A point is 0.5 m from a fixed axis and rotates at 4 rad/s. Its tangential speed is:
A 20 N force acts perpendicular to a wrench 0.25 m from its axis. Torque magnitude is:
quiz.explanation: The perpendicular lever arm is 0.25 m, so torque = 20 x 0.25 = 5 N m.

quiz.question: Doubling a point mass's distance from an axis, keeping its mass fixed, changes its moment of inertia by a factor of:
quiz.explanation: I = mr squared, so doubling r multiplies I by four.

quiz.question: A uniform disk with M = 2 kg and R = 0.5 m has constant net axial torque 1 N m. Starting at rest, its angular speed after 3 s is:
quiz.explanation: I = 0.25 kg m squared, alpha = torque/I = 4 rad/s squared, and omega = alpha t = 12 rad/s.

quiz.question: A uniform solid disk of mass 2 kg rolls without slipping on a stationary surface at centre speed 2 m/s. Its total kinetic energy is:
quiz.explanation: Translational energy is 4 J. Using I = MR squared/2 and omega = v/R gives rotational energy 2 J. Total = 6 J.
